clue.text: Female breaks in tight set — if good service follows it'll do for a Wimbledon champion

indicators.note: something that breaks in forces its way inside, so the female letter goes into the middle of the other group
tight is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of their order

parts.note: the two short words taken as letters to be mixed
G is the usual abbreviation for good
F is the standard abbreviation for female
the Royal Air Force is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A tennis match report: a woman breaks serve in a tight set, and a good serve would make her a Wimbledon winner.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis words (breaks, set, service) all pretend to be about the match. Steffi Graf won Wimbledon seven times; RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force.
explanation.definitionFit: Steffi Graf, the German tennis player, won the Wimbledon ladies' singles title seven times, so she is one example of such a champion.

clue.text: Who killed Cock Robin using extremely sharp weapon?

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the next word, its first and last letters only

parts.note: the two ends of the word sharp
an arrow is a weapon shot from a bow

explanation.surface: A murder-mystery question about the nursery rhyme, asking what sharp weapon did the deed.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, 'Who killed Cock Robin? I, said the Sparrow, with my bow and arrow' — so the weapon in the wordplay really is the one used.
explanation.definitionFit: In the traditional English nursery rhyme the bird that confesses to killing Cock Robin is the sparrow, armed with a bow and arrow.

clue.text: Racecourse out of step, so modernising

indicators.note: the answer comes out of the run of words that follows, taken straight from within them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of step, all of so and the start of modernising

explanation.surface: A racecourse is criticised as behind the times and only now catching up.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom Downs in Surrey is the English racecourse that hosts the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom is a famous English horse-racing venue, home of the Derby, so it is a racecourse by name.

clue.text: Calamity Jane's in town (no firearms fired?)

indicators.note: when something is fired it is blasted apart, so these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: all three words supply letters for the mix

explanation.surface: A Wild West scene: the gunslinging Calamity Jane rides into town, and for once no shots ring out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' looks like it belongs with firearms, but it is the signal to mix town, no and firearms.
explanation.definitionFit: Calamity Jane was a real American woman of the Old West frontier, known as a scout and sharpshooter, so she is an example.

clue.text: Lucky find in middle of boggy, sodden ground

indicators.note: ground means crushed up, as in a mill, so the letters are broken and reformed
middle of asks for only the central letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the third of five letters, the centre of boggy
taken as written, to be mixed

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles on a treasure in the middle of soggy, waterlogged ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' reads as the earth where the find was made, but it is the instruction to mix the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A godsend is something welcome that arrives unexpectedly, like a stroke of good fortune found by chance.

clue.text: Chaos? Some involving bridge

indicators.note: involving means wrapping around, so one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: any, as in 'have you any?', means some
an arch is a bridge-like span

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the card game bridge always ends in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' suggests the card game, but here it is a structure, an arch.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchy is a state of lawlessness and total disorder, a synonym for chaos.

clue.text: Dog with no lead causes irritation

indicators.note: the lead is the front, so having no lead means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a bitch is a female dog

explanation.surface: A dog let off its leash becomes a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' suggests a dog's leash; here it means the leading letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An itch is an irritation of the skin, the urge to scratch.

clue.text: Turtles, partners swimming round island

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the mixed letters go around the island
swimming letters move about freely and settle in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A pair of turtles swim in circles around an island.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrapins are small freshwater turtles, so they are a kind of turtle.

clue.text: Short answer appearing in forceful political publication

indicators.note: appearing in means showing up inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: hard, as in a hard push, means forceful
ans is the shortened form of answer

explanation.surface: A political pamphlet with a forceful tone gives only a curt answer.
explanation.walkthrough: Hansard is the official verbatim record of debates in the UK Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Hansard is the printed transcript of parliamentary proceedings, so it is a publication about politics.

clue.text: What a dark bar may contain?

definitions.text: What a dark bar may contain?

parts.words: What a dark bar may contain?
parts.note: surface reading: a gloomy pub, wondering what it might hold
setter's reading: a bar of dark chocolate, whose contents are simply that kind of sweet

explanation.walkthrough: A 'dark bar' sounds like a dimly lit pub; it is a bar of chocolate. In Britain plain chocolate is the usual name for dark chocolate, with no milk.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain chocolate is British for dark chocolate without milk, and a dark bar of confectionery is made from it.

clue.text: Run off with sailor back out East

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a common crossword sailor

indicators.note: out tells you the named letter is taken away and left outside

parts.note: to second a motion is to back it
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A sailor jumps ship and heads off back out to the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a direction to reverse something; it means support, as in seconding a motion.
explanation.definitionFit: To abscond is to leave secretly and hurriedly, especially to escape, which is to run off.

clue.text: A flap from one lair, well-oiled

indicators.note: well-oiled is slang for drunk, and drunken letters reel into a different order

parts.note: both words supply the letters to mix

explanation.surface: A creature emerges from its lair slick with oil, flapping about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-oiled' sounds like a lubricated hinge, apt for a flap, but it is slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: An aileron is a hinged flap on an aircraft wing, used to control roll.

clue.text: Right occasion to rotate forward

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right

indicators.note: rotating turns the word round so that it reads from the other end

parts.note: a time, as in 'that time', is an occasion

explanation.surface: Instructions for the right moment to turn a vehicle or crop rotation forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' reads as a direction; it is the verb meaning to send on.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit something is to send or pass it on, for example a case to another court, as to forward it.

clue.text: Mexican dish left in hacienda to be cooked

indicators.note: in places one letter inside the other word before the mixing
cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A Mexican dish has been left at a ranch house, waiting to be cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: A hacienda is a large Mexican estate or ranch house, which keeps the surface in Mexico.
explanation.definitionFit: An enchilada is a rolled tortilla with a filling and chilli sauce, a classic Mexican food.

clue.text: Woeful issue?

parts.note: surface reading: a sad matter or problem
setter's reading: issue means offspring, the child of the nursery rhyme who is full of woe

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face' continues 'Wednesday's child is full of woe'. Issue means offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: In the traditional fortune-telling rhyme about birth days, the one born midweek is described as full of woe, a sorrowful offspring.

clue.text: Savage in a Conrad novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are put into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: all three words supply letters

explanation.surface: A literary note about a savage character in one of Joseph Conrad's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book by Conrad, but it is the signal to mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Draconian means excessively harsh or severe, after the Athenian lawgiver Draco, so it can mean savage.

clue.text: A question that may be asked at the bar: why is poor aunt so drunk?

definitions.text: A question that may be asked at the bar

indicators.note: drunk letters lurch out of their order and must be straightened into a new one

parts.note: all five words supply letters

explanation.surface: Someone at the pub wonders why their poor aunt has had so much to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a jocular idiom used by someone buying a round, asking what drink the other person would like.

clue.text: Wife stands, seeing vermin

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
easels are stands for paintings

explanation.surface: A wife freezes on her feet at the sight of pests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stands' reads as a verb; it is the plural noun for frames that hold canvases.
explanation.definitionFit: Weasels are small predatory mammals traditionally regarded by farmers and gamekeepers as vermin.

clue.text: Disgusting old boy linked with ugly incident

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
making a scene is causing an unpleasant public display

explanation.surface: A former pupil is caught up in a disgraceful public row.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscene means offensive to moral standards, repulsive, which is what disgusting means.

clue.text: Peculiar story about Herts town

indicators.note: something peculiar is odd and out of the normal arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be mixed
on, as in a talk on birds, means about

explanation.surface: An odd tale is going round about a town in Hertfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Herts is the abbreviation for Hertfordshire, an English county north of London; Royston is a town in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Royston is a market town in north Hertfordshire, so it is a town in that county.

clue.text: Famous father's come in for a jotter

indicators.note: to have come in is to have entered, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: noted means well known
pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A celebrated dad has dropped by to collect a notebook.
explanation.walkthrough: A jotter is the British word for a small notebook.
explanation.definitionFit: A notepad is a pad of paper for writing notes, the same thing as a jotter.

clue.text: Having loose morals with you, sexually?

indicators.note: loose letters are free to move and settle in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An accusation of loose morals, made in a suggestive tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose morals' reads as a single phrase about promiscuity; loose is the signal to mix morals with you. The question mark flags that the definition is approximate.
explanation.definitionFit: Amorously means in a way showing romantic or sexual desire, so it loosely stands for sexually.

clue.text: Painting style showing circle followed by lines?

parts.note: the letter O is round like a circle
an actor's part is the lines they speak

explanation.surface: An art-class question: is a style made of circles and lines?
explanation.walkthrough: Op art paintings really are built from circles and lines, which is why the question mark is there.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is the 1960s style of abstract painting that uses geometric patterns to create optical illusions.

clue.text: Girl turned up for a valuable thing

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning a word up makes it read from bottom to top, the other way round

parts.note: Tessa is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl arrived carrying something precious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' looks like arrived; in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is a useful or valuable possession or quality.

clue.text: An Arabian state, perhaps, could make me flipping angry!

indicators.note: flipping turns the word over, so it reads backwards

parts.note: taken as written
irate means angry

explanation.surface: An exasperated speaker exclaims that some Gulf state makes them furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word intensifying angry; it is the signal to reverse me.
explanation.definitionFit: An emirate is a territory ruled by an emir, and several Gulf states such as Qatar or Dubai are examples.

clue.text: Cancels Pasteur broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, as seed is, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: the scientist's surname taken as letters

explanation.surface: A TV or radio programme about Louis Pasteur is cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: Louis Pasteur was the French chemist who developed pasteurisation.
explanation.definitionFit: To tear up a contract or agreement is to annul it, so tears up means cancels.

clue.text: Confess offence in front of gendarme, initially

parts.note: a sin is a moral offence

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter only of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of gendarme

explanation.surface: A suspect owns up to a crime in front of a French policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: To sing is slang for confessing or informing to the police. A gendarme is a French police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: In criminal slang to sing is to confess or inform, telling the police everything.

clue.text: Put money back in, control already acquired

parts.note: to rein in is to control
a vested right is one already secured or acquired

explanation.surface: An investor puts profits back into a firm they already control.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinvest is to put returns from an investment into a further investment, putting money back in.
